LOS ANGELES (CNN) -- A group of anonymous software developers said they will soon start selling a program that will allow iPhone owners to use the hugely popular device on cell phone systems around the world and not just with AT&T. Apple's iPhone is yet to go on sale outside the U.S. Apple's iPhone, released in the United States two months ago, was engineered to operate for the first two years only on the AT&T system through an exclusive arrangement between Apple and AT&T. It has not yet been sold outside of the U.S. Los Angeles software consultant Brett Schulte, who is not affiliated with the developers, demonstrated the software for CNN Friday evening. An iPhone that had the new software appeared to work on the T-Mobile system just seconds after Schulte replaced the AT&T SIM card with a T-Mobile SIM card. "It's completely software hacked," Schulte said. "There's no case opening required. It's not required to do any kind of disassembly." It took Schulte about two minutes to unlock the iPhone. The developers would not give CNN their last names, saying "We don't want to be hounded." The said they would start selling the software, which they haven't yet priced, as soon as their online payment and customer service systems are ready. They're also waiting for more information from their lawyers. Apple spokeswoman Jennifer Bowcock told CNN her company has no comment. AT&T spokesman Mark Siegel said he couldn't speculate on the legality of unlocking the phone, but he added, "When you sign up, you're signing a two-year contract. You're obligated to pay the bill." "When people buy the iPhone it's clear from our materials it's designed to operate exclusively on AT&T," Siegel said. Schulte, however, said it is possible to buy an iPhone without being contractually obligated to AT&T. The developers recently created a Web site -- iPhoneSIMfree.com -- but there is very little information on it and no direct way for anyone to purchase the software. Internet records showed they bought the domain name less than two weeks ago. Two members of the group, who identified themselves only as "John" and "Liu," told CNN in a phone interview that a core group of six people on three continents worked to unlock the iPhone as a hobby. They said they are fans of Apple products who thought the iPhone should be made accessible to people who cannot use AT&T. "I'm not in America and I can't use it," said Liu, who would not reveal the country in which he lives. "It's not fair." Asked if he thought modifying the iPhone was legal, he said "That's a very good question. I truly believe it is." John and Liu said they have not been contacted by either Apple or AT&T, but said that could change the moment their software goes on sale. **Anonymous hackers claim breakthrough in unlocking Apple’s iPhone**

*August 2007*

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — A group of anonymous software developers says it has created a program that can unlock Apple’s iPhone, potentially allowing the much-hyped device to be used on mobile phone networks other than AT&T’s in the United States and on carriers around the world.

The iPhone, released in June to long lines and intense media attention, is currently tied exclusively to AT&T’s wireless network under a multiyear agreement with Apple. Customers who buy the phone must activate it through AT&T before using its calling features, a restriction that has frustrated some consumers and drawn interest from technologists eager to open the device to other carriers.

The developers, who have not publicly identified themselves, say their software changes the phone’s internal settings so it will accept SIM cards from other GSM-based carriers. GSM is the dominant mobile standard in much of Europe, Asia and other parts of the world, meaning an unlocked iPhone could potentially be used far beyond Apple’s official launch markets.

The reported breakthrough follows weeks of efforts by independent programmers and hobbyists to examine the iPhone’s software and security protections. Earlier work had allowed some users to activate the device without AT&T service or use it as an iPod and Wi-Fi device, but a full software unlock for phone service has been considered a more significant milestone.

Apple has not announced when the iPhone will be available internationally, though the company has said it plans to expand the product beyond the United States. Industry analysts say unlocking efforts could complicate Apple’s relationships with wireless carriers, which often subsidize or market phones in exchange for exclusive service agreements and revenue-sharing arrangements.

AT&T has declined to comment in detail on unlocking efforts, but the company has emphasized that the iPhone was designed to be used on its network. Apple also has not endorsed third-party unlocking tools and could attempt to disable them through future software updates.

For consumers, the appeal is clear: an unlocked iPhone could be used with a preferred carrier, potentially avoiding roaming charges when traveling abroad or allowing buyers in countries where the iPhone has not yet launched to use the device.

But experts caution that unlocking the phone may void its warranty, violate service agreements or render the device unusable if the process goes wrong. There are also legal uncertainties surrounding the practice, particularly when software is used to bypass technical restrictions placed on a device.

Still, the development underscores the unusual level of attention surrounding Apple’s entry into the mobile phone market. Since its debut, the iPhone has been praised for its touch-screen interface and Web browsing capabilities, while critics have pointed to its high price, lack of 3G data support and exclusive tie to AT&T.

If the anonymous developers’ claims are confirmed and the software spreads widely online, the iPhone could soon appear on networks Apple never officially approved — a sign that, in the age of Internet-connected gadgets, even the most closely managed product launches can be difficult to control.

---

# Early iPhone Unlockers Raise Legal Questions as Apple’s AT&T Deal Faces Workarounds

When Apple introduced the first iPhone in 2007, the device was billed as a breakthrough: a phone, an iPod and an internet communicator combined into one sleek touchscreen product. But for many early buyers, one major limitation quickly became clear — in the United States, the iPhone was locked exclusively to AT&T’s wireless network.

That exclusivity arrangement, a central part of Apple’s initial rollout strategy, meant customers who wanted to use the iPhone on competing carriers had few official options. Almost immediately, a small group of independent developers and hackers began searching for ways around the restriction.

Among them were two developers who agreed to be identified only by the names “John” and “Liu.” They said they worked independently on software designed to unlock the first-generation iPhone, allowing it to operate with SIM cards from carriers other than AT&T.

Their work quickly attracted attention from consumers eager to use Apple’s new device outside AT&T’s network — and raised complicated legal questions about whether unlocking software could be sold commercially.

## A Device Tied to One Carrier

The original iPhone launched at a time when carrier exclusivity agreements were common in the mobile industry. Apple’s partnership with AT&T gave the carrier a major competitive advantage, while Apple gained a distribution partner for its first entry into the phone market.

But the restriction frustrated some consumers, particularly international users and customers in areas where AT&T coverage was weak. Unlike many unlocked phones sold elsewhere in the world, the first iPhone was designed to activate through Apple’s systems and operate on AT&T’s network in the U.S.

That created an opening for developers who believed customers should be able to use hardware they purchased on the network of their choice.

## The Rise of Unlocking Software

John and Liu said their software targeted the technical locks that tied the iPhone to AT&T. While they declined to describe the method in detail, they said the program was intended to allow users to insert another carrier’s SIM card and place calls, send messages and use basic network functions.

“We saw it as giving owners more control over the device,” John said. “People paid for the phone. They wanted to decide where to use it.”

Liu said demand grew quickly once word spread online. “There were people traveling internationally, people who didn’t want AT&T, people who just wanted the option,” Liu said.

But turning an unlocking tool into a paid product introduced a riskier question: Was it legal to sell software that bypassed restrictions built into the phone?

## Legal Uncertainty

The answer was not simple.

At the center of the issue were laws governing copyright, software access controls and consumer rights. In the United States, the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, or DMCA, generally prohibits circumventing certain technological protection measures that control access to copyrighted works. Companies have sometimes argued that software locks fall under those protections.

At the same time, consumer advocates have argued that phone unlocking is a legitimate practice, especially when the goal is interoperability — allowing a device to work on another compatible network.

The legality of unlocking has shifted over time through regulatory exemptions and policy changes. But in the early iPhone era, the landscape was murkier. Developers who sold unlocking tools risked drawing scrutiny from Apple, AT&T or copyright enforcement authorities, particularly if their software modified protected code or bypassed activation systems.

Legal experts have said key questions include whether the tool merely enables network compatibility, whether it circumvents protected software controls, whether it violates terms of service and whether it is distributed for profit.

Selling such software, rather than releasing it freely, could also increase exposure. A commercial product is more visible, may be seen as encouraging breach of contract or circumvention, and could attract lawsuits even where the legal merits are uncertain.

## Apple’s Interest in Control

Apple has historically emphasized tight integration between its hardware, software and services. For the first iPhone, control over activation and carrier access was part of that ecosystem.

Unlocking threatened that model. If large numbers of customers could take iPhones to other carriers, it could undermine the value of Apple’s exclusive arrangement with AT&T and complicate support, updates and network performance.

Neither Apple nor AT&T encouraged unauthorized unlocking. Users who modified their phones also risked losing warranty coverage or encountering problems after software updates.

## Consumer Demand vs. Contract Restrictions

The debate highlighted a broader tension in the mobile industry: once a customer buys a device, how much control should the manufacturer or carrier retain?

Supporters of unlocking said consumers should not be locked into a single carrier indefinitely, especially after paying hundreds of dollars for a phone. Critics argued that carrier subsidies, service agreements and software protections were part of the business model that made the device available on those terms.

John and Liu said they understood the risks but believed the demand reflected a real consumer concern.

“We weren’t trying to damage anyone’s network,” Liu said. “We wanted the phone to be usable.”

## A Precedent for Future Battles

The first iPhone’s unlocking controversy foreshadowed years of debate over jailbreaking, app store restrictions, right-to-repair laws and consumer control over digital devices.

Today, phone unlocking is far more common and is often permitted under specific conditions, particularly once contractual obligations are met. But the early iPhone era remains a key example of how quickly innovation can outpace existing legal frameworks.

For developers like John and Liu, the question was not only whether they could unlock the iPhone, but whether they could legally sell the means to do so.

That question sat at the intersection of technology, copyright law, contract law and consumer rights — and in 2007, it had no easy answer.
